name: The Fundamental Theorem of Galois Theory
aliases: The main theorem of Galois theory
statement: The symmetries of a field's roots mirror its subfields exactly, larger symmetry groups matching smaller fields.
statementAccent: larger symmetry groups matching smaller fields
meaning: The fundamental theorem of Galois theory establishes a precise dictionary between two seemingly different worlds: the subfields lying between a base field and a larger field, and the subgroups of the field's group of symmetries. For a suitable extension, called a Galois extension, there is a one-to-one, inclusion-reversing correspondence between the intermediate fields and the subgroups of the Galois group, the group of automorphisms of the larger field that fix the base field. Bigger subgroups correspond to smaller intermediate fields and the reverse, and normal subgroups correspond to sub-extensions that are themselves Galois. This correspondence translates hard questions about polynomial equations into questions about finite groups, unifying field theory and group theory into one of the most beautiful theorems in mathematics.
mechanism: The Galois group of an extension is the group of field automorphisms of the larger field that leave every element of the base field fixed, permuting the roots of a polynomial among themselves. The theorem sets up two mutually inverse maps: to each intermediate field it assigns the subgroup of automorphisms fixing it, and to each subgroup it assigns its fixed field, the elements left unmoved. These maps reverse inclusions, so the whole group corresponds to the base field and the trivial subgroup to the whole field, and the degree of an intermediate field over the base equals the index of the matching subgroup. A sub-extension is normal, itself Galois, exactly when the corresponding subgroup is normal, in which case the quotient group is the Galois group of that sub-extension.

examples.text: A polynomial is solvable by radicals exactly when its Galois group is a solvable group; the general quintic has Galois group S five, which is not solvable, so no radical formula exists, explaining the Abel-Ruffini theorem.
The theory proves the ancient impossibilities of doubling the cube and trisecting a general angle with straightedge and compass, since these demand field extensions of the wrong degree.
The Gauss-Wantzel theorem, that a regular polygon is constructible exactly when its side count is a power of two times distinct Fermat primes, follows from the same field-theoretic analysis.

variants.name: The infinite Galois correspondence
variants.text: The extension to infinite Galois extensions, where the naive bijection fails and one must equip the profinite Galois group with the Krull topology, matching closed subgroups to intermediate fields.

variants.name: Artin's modern formulation
variants.text: Emil Artin's reworking of the theory around field automorphisms and linear independence rather than permutations of roots, the approach used in most modern textbooks.

whyItMatters: The fundamental theorem of Galois theory is a foundation of modern algebra and algebraic number theory, prized for translating intractable questions about equations into the tractable language of finite groups. Its most celebrated payoff is explaining why the quadratic, cubic, and quartic have general formulas in radicals while the quintic and higher do not, characterising solvability by whether the Galois group is a solvable group, the very source of that term. It resolves the classical impossibilities of Greek geometry and classifies constructible regular polygons, and it seeds the deeper structures, from class field theory to the Langlands programme, that dominate contemporary number theory.

working.text: match intermediate fields with subgroups of the Galois group, reversing inclusions, to turn a field problem into a finite-group problem.
an equation is solvable by radicals exactly when its Galois group is solvable, so the unsolvable S five of the quintic explains the missing formula.
identify which intermediate fields are themselves Galois by finding the normal subgroups, whose quotients give those sub-extensions' groups.

limits: The correspondence in its clean form requires the extension to be Galois, meaning both normal and separable; without those conditions the bijection breaks down. The finite case is the cleanest, and the infinite case needs the Galois group given the Krull topology, with the correspondence then holding only for closed subgroups. The theorem characterises solvability by radicals but does not by itself construct solutions, and the impossibility results it yields are statements about what cannot be done, not recipes. It is a structural bridge, powerful precisely because it reduces field questions to group theory, but it inherits whatever difficulty the resulting group problems carry.
misreadings: The theorem does not itself prove the quintic unsolvable; that existence result is the Abel-Ruffini theorem, which Galois theory explains and characterises through the solvable-group criterion. The correspondence reverses inclusions, so the whole Galois group matches the base field and the trivial subgroup matches the whole field, not the other way around. And it applies to Galois extensions specifically; for a non-normal or inseparable extension the tidy bijection between subfields and subgroups fails, so it is not a universal fact about all field extensions.
origin: Rooted in Evariste Galois's work of around 1830 on the solvability of equations, written up shortly before his death in a duel in 1832 at age twenty and published by Joseph Liouville in 1846; recast in its modern field-and-automorphism form by Emil Artin in the twentieth century.
